segments.video_title: Columbus, Vasco da Gama, and Zheng He - 15th Century Mariners: Crash Course World History #21

vocab.definition: Let sailors find direction with no land in sight, so they no longer had to hug the coast.
A Greek/Islamic tool for measuring the height of stars, which gave sailors their latitude.
A small, nimble Portuguese ship mixing southern European and North African designs. It was built for long open-ocean voyages.
A triangular sail that let caravels sail closer to the wind.
A bigger, sturdier ship than the caravel. It could carry more supplies, stay at sea longer and survive the Atlantic.
A detailed nautical map showing coastlines, harbors and compass directions.
Working out your position from direction, speed and time (timed with an hourglass). It was Columbus’s main navigation method.

segments.video_title: Columbus, Vasco da Gama, and Zheng He - 15th Century Mariners: Crash Course World History #21

segments.label: Prince Henry, da Gama, and the Portuguese “trading post empire”
segments.video_title: Columbus, Vasco da Gama, and Zheng He - 15th Century Mariners: Crash Course World History #21

vocab.definition: Ming admiral who led 7 huge Indian Ocean voyages (1405–1433): 300+ ships, 27,000 crew, flagships 400+ ft long.
Foreign rulers bowed to the Chinese emperor (the kowtow) and gave him gifts in exchange for the right to trade with China.
Portuguese prince who wasn’t a navigator himself. He funded sailors and collected nautical knowledge and maps.
First of Henry’s protégés to round Africa. He reached Calicut, India in 1498 looking for “gold and Christians.”
Portugal didn’t take big territory in the Indian Ocean. It captured fortified coastal cities and controlled trade from them.
A Portuguese trade permit that merchant ships were forced to buy, or risk capture. Basically extortion.

segments.label: Cajamarca 1532: the Requerimiento, a thrown Bible, and an ambush
segments.video_title: Spanish Conquest of the Incan Empire

vocab.definition: Pope Alexander VI settled a Spain–Portugal dispute by splitting the world’s “unclaimed” land between the two.
Spanish conqueror in the Americas, like Cortés (Aztecs) or Pizarro (Inca).
The supreme ruler of the Inca Empire, treated as a god. Without him the empire couldn’t function.
A Spanish document read aloud to Native peoples: accept the Church and the king or face war and slavery.
Indigenous woman who spoke Maya and Nahuatl and became Cortés’s interpreter. Language was a weapon as important as horses or cannons.
A city-state permanently at war with the Aztecs. It allied with Cortés, and his army ended up less than 5% Spanish.

segments.label: Disease: why 50–90% of Native Americans died
segments.video_title: The Columbian Exchange: Crash Course World History #23

segments.label: Animals: pigs, horses, oxen remake the Americas
segments.video_title: The Columbian Exchange: Crash Course World History #23

segments.label: Plants: New World crops feed the Old World
segments.video_title: The Columbian Exchange: Crash Course World History #23

vocab.definition: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases and people between the Old World and the New World after 1492.
The deadliest Old World disease in the Americas. With other diseases it killed most Native Americans, who had no immunity.
Calorie-dense American crops that boosted Old World populations: potatoes in Europe, manioc (cassava) in Africa, sweet potatoes in China.
Pigs, horses, cattle and oxen brought by Europeans that reshaped American land and Native life.

segments.label: Sakoku: why Tokugawa Japan kicked out everyone but the Dutch
segments.video_title: Why did Japan ban everyone except for the Dutch? (Short Animated Documentary)

vocab.definition: The military government that unified Japan after a civil war in the early 1600s and moved to control foreign contact.
Japan’s policy of strictly limiting foreign trade and contact. Only the Dutch could trade, and only through Nagasaki.
The one port open to the Dutch East India Company, which had to follow Japanese rules and never preach Christianity.

topics.title: Labor shortage → the Atlantic slave trade

segments.label: The numbers: 10–12 million, mostly to Brazil & the Caribbean
segments.video_title: The Atlantic Slave Trade: Crash Course World History #24

segments.label: How Europeans got enslaved Africans + life on a sugar plantation
segments.video_title: The Atlantic Slave Trade: Crash Course World History #24

segments.label: Why Atlantic slavery was different: chattel slavery
segments.video_title: The Atlantic Slave Trade: Crash Course World History #24

segments.label: Effects on Africa + the birth of racial ideology
segments.video_title: The Atlantic slave trade: What too few textbooks told you - Anthony Hazard

vocab.definition: About 10–12 million Africans were shipped to the Americas from 1500 to 1880, most to Brazil and the Caribbean.
Enslaved people treated as movable property, bought and sold. Atlantic slavery was built on this.
The deadly Atlantic crossing on slave ships: about 4 square feet per person, “not so much room as a man in his coffin.”
The main destination of enslaved labor in Brazil and the Caribbean: brutal work, 48-hour shifts at harvest.
To justify slavery, Europeans claimed Africans were biologically inferior, which gave slavery a racial basis.

segments.label: Who “won” the Indian Ocean? Ottoman vs Portuguese scorecard
segments.video_title: Ottoman-Portuguese War for the Indian Ocean - DOCUMENTARY

vocab.definition: The Dutch East India Company: one chartered company given a monopoly on East Indies trade. It could hire its own people and wage war, and investors owned it through shares.
Owning a small piece of a company, which spread the risk of a voyage across many investors.
The VOC used force to become the only seller of spices like nutmeg and cloves. Coen: “no trade without war.”
Colonies supply raw materials and buy manufactured goods, and may trade only with the mother country, so wealth flows to Europe.
A Muslim–European struggle over Indian Ocean trade. The Ottomans used corsair raids and the Portuguese used fortified ports.

segments.label: Maroons: the free communities of the Great Dismal Swamp
segments.video_title: The Hidden Black Society They Don’t Teach You About

vocab.definition: The Inca labor draft that Spain adapted for its silver mountain: 1 in 7 adult Native men per district mined for a year at subsistence wages.
American silver flooded Spain and Europe, money lost value and prices soared.
Spanish ships carried American silver across the Pacific to buy Chinese goods. Ming China wanted silver for taxes, creating the first global market.
Britain vs. France (1756–1763), fought worldwide over trade and colonies. Britain won, but its war debt led to the taxes behind the American Revolution.
Metacom of Pokanoket (the English called him “King Philip”) led a coalition of tribes against encroaching New England colonists. Per capita it was the bloodiest war in American history.
Native Americans converted to Christianity and settled in colonial “praying towns,” which deepened tensions.
Ruler of Ndongo/Matamba (Angola) who spent 40 years resisting Portuguese slaving and conquest through diplomacy and war.
People who escaped slavery and built free, hidden communities, like the Great Dismal Swamp, which lasted 250+ years.

segments.label: The casta system: peninsulares vs. criollos
segments.video_title: The “Casta” System

segments.label: Syncretism in action: lwa = saints, and Kongo’s King Afonso
segments.video_title: Vodou: Haiti's African-Derived Religion

vocab.definition: Spain’s legal racial hierarchy in its colonies. Your mix of Spanish, Native and African ancestry decided your rights and jobs.
Spaniards born in Spain. They held the top jobs: viceroys, governors, bishops.
Spaniards born in the Americas. They were trusted less and kept out of the highest posts.
Mixed Spanish–Native (mestizo) and Spanish–African (mulatto) people, ranked below Spaniards in the casta system.
Haitian religion blending West African traditions with Catholicism. Spirits (lwa) are equated with Catholic saints.
The spirits served in Vodou, also called saints or mysteries.

vocab.term: Kingdom of Kongo / King Afonso I
vocab.definition: A Central African kingdom that became Catholic in 1491–1509, so Africans were blending Catholicism with ancestral religion before the Atlantic crossing.
Louis XIV’s rules for treating enslaved people in French colonies, including forced conversion to Christianity.

vocab.definition: Church documents sold to reduce time in purgatory, which was Luther’s main complaint.
Luther’s 1517 list of arguments against the Church, posted on the Wittenberg church door for debate.
